Baseline · weeks 1–8 · one average per store

← Return to the worked analysis

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

Use the same analysis rows

The baseline profile is an average of eight weekly percentages for each store. Equal monitoring exposure and equal weeks give every store the same weight in the overall average.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Group mean = sum of store baseline rates divided by stores in the group. Above-target share = count(baseline_rate > 10) divided by that group’s store count. Quantiles are calculated across store averages, not across all weekly rows.

stores = world()['stores']
worked_mean = stores.baseline_rate.mean()
summary = stores.groupby('risk_group').baseline_rate.agg(['count','mean','median'])
above = stores.assign(above=stores.baseline_rate > 10).groupby('risk_group').above.mean()
assert np.isclose(worked_mean, lesson_result(2)['mean'])

# Inspect distribution and association using the same store profiles.
stores = world()['stores']
rates = stores.baseline_rate.to_numpy()
counts, edges = np.histogram(rates, bins=np.arange(0, 36, 4))
assert counts.sum() == 150
sample_sd = rates.std(ddof=1)
correlation = np.corrcoef(stores.baseline_demand, rates)[0,1]
assert np.isclose(sample_sd, lesson_result(2)['depth']['sd'])
assert np.isclose(correlation, lesson_result(2)['depth']['correlation'])

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

These are descriptive summaries of the complete baseline release. They do not require a sampling interval to describe that release. Uncertainty about a new audit or future outcomes is introduced separately in Lessons 3 and 6.

Change one analytical choice

Change the service target to 12% or 15% and recalculate group coverage. Explain how the operational review workload changes even though the underlying distribution stays fixed.

Probability gives distributions a language

From an observation to a random variable

  • A random variable assigns a numerical outcome to an uncertain event.
  • A probability distribution describes possible values and their probabilities.
  • Expected value averages outcomes using probability weights.

A stockout indicator takes values zero and one; a weekly stockout count takes integer values; a planning error can be treated as continuous. Empirical distributions summarize observed frequencies. Theoretical distributions are models used to reason about repetition and uncertainty.

Choose a model for its mechanism
ModelBusiness interpretationKey distinction
Bernoulli(p)One product-day is or is not unavailableTwo possible outcomes
Binomial(n,p)Count across n independent equal-probability opportunitiesRequires a specified n and p
UniformAn equal-chance draw over a rangeUsed by the teaching generator
NormalA symmetric model for continuous variationUnbounded, determined by mean and variance
LognormalA positive quantity whose logarithm is normalRight-skewed
ParetoA positive heavy-tail modelLarge values can retain substantial probability

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), when P(B) > 0

Bernoulli: E[X] = p, Var(X) = p(1−p); Binomial: E[X] = np, Var(X) = np(1−p)

For a discrete random variable, sum its value times the probability at that value to obtain its expectation. A probability mass function assigns probabilities to discrete values; a probability density assigns probability through areas over intervals. For a binomial count, P(X=k) = choose(n,k) p^k (1−p)^(n−k).

Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). A latent variable is unobserved, such as an underlying store capability; a proxy is an observed measure intended to inform us about it. More data or a more flexible AI model does not by itself establish the causal direction of a correlation.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

All 150 store profiles are calculated from the same eight repaired weekly records per store. The group comparison introduces no new dataset and changes no stockout definition.
